title: PM Pitfall: Sellers Weren't Churning Over a Bug
description:
Seven support tickets and a churn-exit interview all pointed at the same 'broken' feature -- but the real cause wasn't a bug, it was an undocumented delay nobody told users about. This is the pitfall hiding inside the sample scenario from the Product Manager Mastery Path's Level 1 capstone project: writing a complete PRD. Before you write a single requirement, your problem statement has to name the real problem -- and it's rarely the one users think they're reporting.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/product-manager-mastery-path/level-1/10-project-complete-prd/

#Shorts

beats.narration: Seven support tickets and one churn interview, all pointing at the same 'bug.'

display.heading: The Tickets All Said 'Broken'
display.subheading: Product Manager Mastery Path -- Level 1 Capstone

beats.narration: Turns out Marketplace B's price sync just runs four to six hours late -- and nobody ever told the sellers that.

display.heading: The real cause
display.subheading: A 4-6 hour sync delay, completely undocumented

beats.narration: So sellers weren't churning over a slow sync. They were churning because prices looked wrong with zero explanation -- and that's what killed their trust.

display.heading: The pitfall
display.subheading: Not a speed problem -- a trust problem

beats.narration: Jump straight to 'fix the delay' and you've fixed the wrong problem. A real problem statement has to prove which one it actually is before anyone writes a requirement.

display.heading: Before you write one requirement
display.subheading: Name the real problem, not the reported symptom
